title: 9.1 Small Group · Group 2
contentObjective: I can recognize when two quantities change together, and identify which one is the independent variable and which is the dependent variable, explain how I can tell, and judge a case I have not seen before.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

turnAndTalk.question: Akela put her three bean trays in three different spots, so each got a different amount of sunlight. After three weeks she measured the height of the plants. Which of those two quantities did Akela choose, and which one responded?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Akela chose where to place each tray, which set the hours of sunlight; the plant height was measured afterward, in response to the sunlight.

turnAndTalk.question: At the pizza shop, the number of employees (6) and the topping limit (3) stay fixed no matter how many pizzas are made, but the cost of cheese changes with every pizza. Why do employees and toppings NOT count as part of a dependent relationship here?
turnAndTalk.kernel: A dependent relationship needs a quantity that actually changes in response to another; a fixed number like 6 employees never changes, so it can't depend on anything.

extendStems: No, because the number of employees ___ no matter how many pizzas are made.
A variable can ___, but a fixed quantity stays ___.

turnAndTalk.question: Look back at a practice problem where you had to name the independent and dependent variable. What question did you ask yourself first?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The test for independent is 'who or what gets to choose this quantity' — the other quantity is dependent because it responds.

launch.narrative: This is your challenge small group for Lesson 9.1. You can already get the answer — so in here the answer is the starting point. We ask when the method holds, when it breaks, and how you would convince someone who disagrees.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — Which quantity is doing the changing — and which is responding?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. So we go up a level, not up a number: find what is always true, show it a second way, and be ready to defend it with a reason instead of an answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: The independent variable is subject to choice. The dependent variable changes in response to it — and you can say why it is true, and where it would stop being true.

connect.scenario: At a local pizza shop a customer can order up to three toppings on a large pizza. The shop has 6 employees. The shop spends $1.15 on cheese and $1.95 on sauce for each pizza it makes.
connect.promptQuestion: Which two quantities in this shop are related, so that one depends on the other — and which quantity does NOT depend on the number of pizzas at all?
connect.prompt: In this scenario, the ___ is the independent variable. The ___ and the ___ both depend on it. The number of ___ stays the same no matter how many pizzas are made.

check.stem: The number of pizzas made each week determines other costs at the shop. Which variable is the independent variable in this relationship?
check.explanation: The number of pizzas is independent because it is the value that determines the other costs. Cost of cheese is dependent because it changes as a result of pizzas made; the number of employees and toppings allowed are fixed limits, not quantities that change with pizza count.

check.stem: Which two quantities have a dependent relationship in this scenario?
choices: cost of cheese and number of pizzas made
number of employees and number of pizzas made
number of toppings allowed and cost of sauce
number of employees and number of toppings allowed
check.explanation: The cost of cheese rises as more pizzas are made ($1.15 per pizza), so it depends on the number of pizzas. The number of employees (6) and the topping limit (3) are fixed values that stay the same no matter how many pizzas are made, so they are not part of a dependent relationship here.

check.stem: The shop makes 20 pizzas in a week. Which of these does NOT depend on the number of pizzas sold?
choices: the total spent on cheese and sauce combined
check.explanation: Staff count (6 employees) is fixed and stays the same regardless of pizza volume. Cheese cost, sauce cost, and their combined total all scale up as more pizzas are made, so those three DO depend on the number of pizzas.

connect.modelAnswer: The cost of cheese each week depends on the number of pizzas the shop makes, so the number of pizzas is the independent variable and the cheese cost is the dependent variable. The number of employees is 6 no matter how many pizzas are sold, so it does not depend on the number of pizzas.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — A dog walker charges by the hour. Which sentence is correct?
choices: The total charge depends on the number of hours, so hours is the independent variable.
The number of hours depends on the total charge, so the charge is the independent variable.
Neither quantity depends on the other.
exitTicket.explanation: The walker chooses how many hours to work; the money that results responds to that choice. Hours is subject to choice, so hours is independent and the total charge is dependent.
hints: Which one does someone get to CHOOSE?

The quantity that responds is the dependent one.

onLevel.stem: Which question would you ask to find the DEPENDENT variable?

onLevel.explanation: The dependent variable is defined by its response to the independent variable — not by size, units, or name.
choiceFeedback: Size has nothing to do with which variable is dependent.
Both quantities usually have units.
Alphabetical order has nothing to do with mathematics here.
hints: Go back to the definition.

Both quantities still change and are still related.
You have the two variables backward. Ask which one someone gets to CHOOSE — that one is independent.

extending.stem: Two quantities are related. Which statement is ALWAYS true?

Dependent variables can be centimeters, Calories, miles — anything that responds.
Table layout is a convention, not a definition.

extending.stem: A pizza shop decides each morning how many pizzas to make, then weighs out the cheese it needs. Devon says: “Cheese is the independent variable, because the shop buys the cheese before it makes any pizzas.” Devon is wrong. What rule did Devon use, and why does that rule fail here?
extending.stemEs: Una pizzería decide cada mañana cuántas pizzas va a hacer y luego pesa el queso que necesita. Devon dice: “El queso es la variable independiente, porque la pizzería compra el queso antes de hacer las pizzas”. Devon está equivocado. ¿Qué regla usó Devon y por qué esa regla falla aquí?
extending.modelAnswer: Devon used the rule “whatever happens first in time is the independent variable.” That rule fails because the roles depend on what is chosen, not on what happens first. The shop chooses the number of pizzas, so pizzas is the independent variable, and the cheese used responds to that choice — cheese is dependent.
extending.modelAnswerEs: Devon usó la regla “lo que ocurre primero en el tiempo es la variable independiente”. Esa regla falla porque los papeles dependen de lo que se elige, no de lo que ocurre primero. La pizzería elige el número de pizzas, así que las pizzas son la variable independiente, y el queso usado responde a esa elección — el queso es dependiente.
sentenceStems: That rule fails because the independent variable is the one that ___ .
Here the shop chooses ___ , so ___ depends on ___ .
sentenceStemsEs: Esa regla falla porque la variable independiente es la que ___ .
Aquí la pizzería elige ___ , así que ___ depende de ___ .

extending.stem: Claim: “The dependent variable always has the larger values.” Is this claim always, sometimes, or never true?
extending.stemEs: Afirmación: “La variable dependiente siempre tiene los valores más grandes”. ¿Esta afirmación es siempre, a veces o nunca verdadera?
choices: Sometimes — the size of the numbers has nothing to do with which variable is which
Always — the dependent variable is the result, so it is bigger
Never — the independent variable is always the larger one
Only when both quantities are measured in the same unit
choicesEs: A veces — el tamaño de los números no tiene nada que ver con cuál variable es cuál
Siempre — la variable dependiente es el resultado, así que es más grande
Nunca — la variable independiente siempre es la más grande
Solo cuando ambas cantidades se miden en la misma unidad
extending.explanation: Sometimes. Jog for 90 minutes and you might run 9 miles — the dependent value (9) is smaller. Give a plant 3 hours of sunlight and it might reach 12 cm — the dependent value (12) is larger. The role is decided by which quantity is subject to choice, not by which numbers are bigger.
extending.explanationEs: A veces. Si trotas 90 minutos podrías correr 9 millas — el valor dependiente (9) es más pequeño. Si le das a una planta 3 horas de sol podría llegar a 12 cm — el valor dependiente (12) es más grande. El papel lo decide cuál cantidad se elige, no cuáles números son más grandes.
choiceFeedback: Find one case where the dependent value is smaller — 90 minutes of jogging, 9 miles run — and the claim breaks.
That is the same mistake in reverse. Try to find a case where the dependent value is larger.
Units do not decide the roles either. 90 minutes → 9 miles uses different units and the dependent value is still smaller.
hints: Try to find ONE example where the claim is false. One is enough to rule out “always”.
Jog 90 minutes and run 9 miles. Which value is larger — the one you chose, or the one that responded?
hintsEs: Intenta encontrar UN ejemplo donde la afirmación sea falsa. Uno basta para descartar “siempre”.
Trota 90 minutos y corre 9 millas. ¿Cuál valor es más grande — el que elegiste o el que respondió?

extending.stem: Describe one situation where time is the independent variable, and a different situation where time is the dependent variable. For each one, say who or what does the choosing.
extending.stemEs: Describe una situación donde el tiempo sea la variable independiente y una situación distinta donde el tiempo sea la variable dependiente. En cada una, di quién o qué hace la elección.
extending.modelAnswer: Independent: I choose to jog for 30 minutes and see how many Calories I burn. I chose the time, so time is independent and Calories depend on it. Dependent: I run exactly 3 miles and record how long it takes. I chose the distance, so time responded — time is dependent. Same quantity, opposite roles, because a different thing was chosen each time.
extending.modelAnswerEs: Independiente: elijo trotar 30 minutos y veo cuántas calorías quemo. Yo elegí el tiempo, así que el tiempo es independiente y las calorías dependen de él. Dependiente: corro exactamente 3 millas y registro cuánto tardo. Yo elegí la distancia, así que el tiempo respondió — el tiempo es dependiente. La misma cantidad, papeles opuestos, porque en cada caso se eligió algo distinto.
sentenceStems: Time is independent when ___ chooses ___ , and ___ responds.
Time is dependent when ___ chooses ___ , and the time responds.
sentenceStemsEs: El tiempo es independiente cuando ___ elige ___ , y ___ responde.
El tiempo es dependiente cuando ___ elige ___ , y el tiempo responde.

extending.stem: Here is the result of an experiment: “Water temperature depends on how long the pot has been on the stove.” Working backwards, describe the experiment. What would you choose, what would you measure, and what would the two column headings of your table be?
extending.stemEs: Este es el resultado de un experimento: “La temperatura del agua depende de cuánto tiempo lleva la olla en la estufa”. Trabajando al revés, describe el experimento. ¿Qué elegirías, qué medirías y cuáles serían los dos encabezados de las columnas de tu tabla?
extending.modelAnswer: I would choose the number of minutes the pot stays on the stove — that is the independent variable, because I decide it. I would measure the water temperature at each of those times — that is the dependent variable, because it responds. My table's columns would be “Minutes on the stove” and “Water temperature (°C)”, with the chosen quantity in the first column.
extending.modelAnswerEs: Elegiría el número de minutos que la olla permanece en la estufa — esa es la variable independiente, porque yo la decido. Mediría la temperatura del agua en cada uno de esos momentos — esa es la variable dependiente, porque responde. Las columnas de mi tabla serían “Minutos en la estufa” y “Temperatura del agua (°C)”, con la cantidad elegida en la primera columna.
sentenceStems: I would choose ___ , so that is the ___ variable.
I would measure ___ , so that is the ___ variable.
My two columns would be ___ and ___ .
sentenceStemsEs: Yo elegiría ___ , así que esa es la variable ___ .
Yo mediría ___ , así que esa es la variable ___ .

practice.commonMistake: Naming the variables backward — calling the responding quantity 'independent' because it is the one the question asks about.

x is multiplied by 4, so divide both sides by 4: 32 ÷ 4 = 8.

questions.stem: Maya needs at least 20 points to win a prize. Which inequality shows this?
questions.explanation: "At least 20" includes 20 itself, so the symbol must allow equal to: p ≥ 20.
7 is added to x, so subtract 7 from both sides: 19 − 7 = 12.

parallelPractice.stem: Movie tickets cost $3 each. The table pairs tickets bought (x) with total cost (y). Complete the table, then name the variable that DEPENDS on the other — type cost or tickets.

steps.prompt: The total changes BECAUSE the tickets change, so the dependent variable is the ___ (type cost or tickets).
steps.promptEs: El total cambia PORQUE cambian los boletos, así que la variable dependiente es ___ (escribe cost o tickets).

hints: Re-read the question. What exactly is it asking you to find?
Ask which quantity you choose first, and which one is decided FOR you by that choice.
